notes.definition: When a wave meets a boundary between two different materials it can be reflected (bounce back), absorbed (its energy is transferred to the material) or transmitted (pass through, often changing direction by refraction). For reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
explanation: Whenever a wave reaches the boundary between two different materials, three things can happen. It can be reflected, meaning it bounces back from the surface. It can be absorbed, meaning its energy is transferred to the energy store of the material, which usually warms up. Or it can be transmitted, meaning it passes through the material and carries on, often changing direction (refraction). Often a mixture of all three happens: a window transmits most light but reflects some, which is why you can see a faint reflection in it.

What happens depends on the substance and on the wavelength of the wave. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet. A brick wall reflects and absorbs light but transmits radio waves, which is why a radio works indoors. A dark, matt surface absorbs most of the light that falls on it, while a white or shiny surface reflects most of it.

Reflection can be shown with a ray diagram. A ray is a straight line with an arrow showing the direction the wave travels. At the point where the ray meets the surface, draw the normal: a dashed line at 90° to the surface. The angle of incidence (i) is the angle between the incoming ray and the normal; the angle of reflection (r) is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. The law of reflection states that i = r. Always measure angles from the normal, not from the surface.

A smooth surface such as a mirror gives a clear reflection because all the rays obey i = r and the parallel rays stay parallel after reflection. A rough surface, such as paper, still obeys i = r at each tiny point, but the normals point in many directions, so the reflected rays are scattered and no clear image is formed.

Required practical 9 investigates the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances. A ray box with a single slit produces a narrow beam in a darkened room. For reflection, the ray is shone at a plane mirror at different angles; the rays are marked with crosses on paper, the normal is drawn, and the angles are measured with a protractor. For refraction, a rectangular block of glass or acrylic is traced on paper, a ray is shone into it, the entry and exit points are marked and joined, and the angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal. Light bends towards the normal entering glass and away from the normal leaving it.
keyFacts: At a boundary a wave can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
What happens depends on the substance and the wavelength of the wave.
The normal is a construction line at 90° to the surface where the ray hits it.
Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
Angles are always measured between the ray and the normal, not the surface.
Smooth surfaces give a clear reflection; rough surfaces scatter the light.
Transmitted light may be refracted: towards the normal when entering glass from air, away from it when leaving.
Required practical 9 uses a ray box, mirror, glass or acrylic blocks, protractor and a darkened room.
Absorbed wave energy increases the internal energy of the material, so it warms up.

keyTerms.definition: When a wave bounces back from a boundary between two materials.
When a wave's energy is transferred to the material it meets, so the wave does not continue.
When a wave passes through a material and continues travelling.
An imaginary line drawn at right angles (90°) to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
The angle between the incident (incoming) ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
A lamp in a box with a slit that produces a narrow beam (ray) of light for ray diagrams.

workedExamples.title: Angles measured from the surface
workedExamples.question: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the surface of the mirror is 25°. What is the angle of reflection?
steps: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror.
By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 65°.

workedExamples.title: Drawing a reflection ray diagram
workedExamples.question: Describe how to draw the reflected ray when a ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°.
steps: Draw the mirror as a straight line and mark the point where the ray hits it.
Use a protractor to draw the normal at 90° to the mirror through that point (dashed line).
Draw the incident ray at 30° to the normal, with an arrow pointing towards the mirror.
Measure 30° on the other side of the normal and draw the reflected ray, with an arrow pointing away from the mirror.
workedExamples.answer: The reflected ray leaves at 30° to the normal on the opposite side of the normal to the incident ray.

workedExamples.title: Deciding what happens at a boundary
workedExamples.question: A student shines a torch at a sheet of frosted glass. Some light is seen on the far side, the glass warms slightly and a faint patch of light is seen on the torch side. Identify each process.
steps: Light seen on the far side has passed through: transmission.
The glass warming shows energy was transferred to it: absorption.
Light seen on the torch side has bounced back: reflection.
workedExamples.answer: Transmission, absorption and reflection are all taking place.

diagrams.title: Reflection from a plane mirror
diagrams.caption: The normal is drawn at 90° to the mirror. The angle of incidence (i) equals the angle of reflection (r), both measured from the normal.

diagrams.title: Refraction through a glass block (required practical 9)
diagrams.caption: A ray from a ray box bends towards the normal as it enters the glass (r is smaller than i) and away from the normal as it leaves. The emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often measure the angle of incidence from the surface of the mirror.
misconceptions.right: In fact both angles are measured from the normal, the line at 90° to the surface.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think rough surfaces do not obey the law of reflection.
misconceptions.right: In fact each point on a rough surface obeys i = r, but the normals point in different directions so the light is scattered.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a wave is only reflected or only transmitted.
misconceptions.right: In fact most boundaries partly reflect, partly absorb and partly transmit a wave; the proportions depend on the material and the wavelength.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think light always bends towards the normal at a boundary.
misconceptions.right: In fact light bends towards the normal when it slows down (air into glass) and away from it when it speeds up (glass into air).

realWorld: Mirrors in cars and periscopes use the law of reflection to let drivers and submarine crews see objects out of their direct line of sight.
Road signs and cycle reflectors are designed to reflect car headlights back towards the driver.
Sound-absorbing panels in recording studios and cinemas reduce reflection (echoes) from walls.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic, including required practical 9 (reflection and refraction of light), is in separate Physics only.
Waves may be reflected, absorbed or transmitted at the boundary between two materials, depending on the substance and the wavelength.
Construct ray diagrams to show the reflection of a wave at a surface.
examTips: Always draw the normal as a dashed line at 90° to the surface and put arrows on rays to show the direction of travel.
If a question gives the angle to the surface, subtract it from 90° to get the angle to the normal.
In required practical 9, explain that a darkened room and a narrow ray make the ray easier to see and mark accurately, and marking the ray with crosses far apart reduces errors in drawing it.
Use a sharp pencil and a protractor; describe drawing round the glass block before removing it to draw the ray inside.
Use the three key words precisely: reflected, absorbed, transmitted.
summary: At a boundary, waves can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
The outcome depends on the material and the wavelength.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal.
Smooth surfaces reflect clearly; rough surfaces scatter light.
Required practical 9: ray box, mirror and glass block, angles measured with a protractor.

questions.question: A wave meets a boundary and its energy is transferred to the material, which warms up. What has happened to the wave?
options: It has been reflected
It has been transmitted
It has been absorbed
It has been refracted
markScheme: 1 mark: It has been absorbed
questions.explanation: Absorption transfers the wave's energy to the material. Reflection sends it back, transmission lets it pass through, and refraction is a change in direction of a transmitted wave.

questions.question: What is the law of reflection?
options: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Angle of incidence = 90° − angle of reflection
Angle of reflection is always 90°
Angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
markScheme: 1 mark: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
questions.explanation: For any reflecting surface the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

questions.question: In a ray diagram, what is the normal?
options: The line along the surface of the mirror
The path of the reflected ray
A line parallel to the incident ray
A line at 90° to the surface where the ray hits it
markScheme: 1 mark: A line at 90° to the surface where the ray hits it
questions.explanation: The normal is a construction line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence. Angles are measured from it.

questions.question: A ray of light strikes a mirror. The angle between the ray and the mirror surface is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
markScheme: 1 mark: 55°
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is from the normal: 90° − 35° = 55°. The angle of reflection equals this, 55°. Choosing 35° comes from measuring from the surface.

questions.question: Why can you see a clear image in a mirror but not in a sheet of white paper?
options: The paper absorbs all the light
The paper is rough so reflected rays are scattered in many directions
The paper does not obey the law of reflection
The paper transmits all the light
markScheme: 1 mark: The paper is rough so reflected rays are scattered in many directions
questions.explanation: Paper reflects most light (that is why it looks white), but its rough surface scatters the rays. Each tiny part still obeys i = r.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect whether a wave is reflected, absorbed or transmitted at a boundary?
options: The type of material
The wavelength of the wave
The nature of the surface (rough or smooth)
The distance the wave has travelled before reaching the boundary
markScheme: 1 mark: The distance the wave has travelled before reaching the boundary
questions.explanation: The spec states that what happens depends on the substance and the wavelength; surface texture also matters. The distance already travelled does not change what happens at the boundary.

questions.question: In required practical 9, why is a ray box with a narrow slit used?
options: To produce a thin ray whose path can be marked accurately
To make the light brighter by focusing it
To change the wavelength of the light
To stop the light being reflected
markScheme: 1 mark: To produce a thin ray whose path can be marked accurately
questions.explanation: A single narrow ray gives a clear line whose centre can be marked with crosses, so angles can be measured accurately.

questions.question: A ray passes from air into a glass block. Which statement is correct?
options: The angle of refraction is larger than the angle of incidence
The ray does not change direction at any angle
The angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence
The ray bends away from the normal
markScheme: 1 mark: The angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence
questions.explanation: Light slows down in glass, so it bends towards the normal: the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence (unless the ray is along the normal, when it does not bend).

questions.question: A student measures the angle of reflection from a mirror to be 2° larger than the angle of incidence every time. What is the most likely cause?
options: A random error from reading the protractor
The mirror does not obey the law of reflection
The light was absorbed by the mirror
A systematic error, such as the normal being drawn slightly away from 90°
markScheme: 1 mark: A systematic error, such as the normal being drawn slightly away from 90°
questions.explanation: A consistent difference in the same direction every time points to a systematic error. A badly drawn normal adds to one angle and subtracts from the other.

questions.question: A ray hits a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 42°. State the angle of reflection.
markScheme: 1 mark: 42°
questions.explanation: By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 42°.

questions.question: A ray of light makes an angle of 28° with the surface of a mirror. Calculate the angle of incidence.
markScheme: 1 mark: 62°
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the surface: 90° − 28° = 62°.

questions.question: The angle of incidence on a mirror is 35°. Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray.
markScheme: 1 mark: angle of reflection = 35°
1 mark: total angle = 35 + 35 = 70°
questions.explanation: The reflected ray is 35° on the other side of the normal, so the angle between the two rays is 35° + 35° = 70°.

questions.question: The angle between an incident ray and its reflected ray is 110°. Calculate the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror surface.
markScheme: 1 mark: angle of reflection = 110 ÷ 2 = 55°
1 mark: angle to surface = 90 − 55 = 35°
questions.explanation: The normal bisects the angle between the rays, so r = 55°. The angle to the surface is 90° − 55° = 35°.

questions.question: Name three things that can happen to a wave when it meets the boundary between two materials.
markScheme: 1 mark: reflected
1 mark: absorbed
1 mark: transmitted
questions.explanation: Waves can be reflected, absorbed or transmitted. Often all three happen to different extents.

questions.question: State the two factors that the AQA specification says determine whether a wave is reflected, absorbed or transmitted.
markScheme: 1 mark: the substance / material AND the wavelength of the wave (both needed)
questions.explanation: Different materials, and different wavelengths, behave differently at a boundary.

questions.question: In required practical 9, a student uses a ray box and plane mirror. Explain how she should record the paths of the rays so that the angles can be measured accurately.
acceptedAnswers: mark ray with crosses far apart
markScheme: 1 mark: mark the incident and reflected rays with two (or more) crosses, far apart
1 mark: join the crosses with a ruler and draw the normal at 90° using a protractor
questions.explanation: Crosses far apart reduce the error in the direction of the line; the normal must be accurate because both angles are measured from it.

questions.question: Explain why a brick wall allows a radio to work indoors but you cannot see through it.
acceptedAnswers: brick absorbs or reflects visible light
markScheme: 1 mark: brick transmits radio waves (long wavelength)
1 mark: brick absorbs / reflects visible light
questions.explanation: Whether a wave is transmitted depends on the wavelength as well as the material. Long-wavelength radio waves pass through walls; light does not.

questions.question: Suggest why a student should repeat the refraction measurements in required practical 9 using blocks of different materials but the same shape.
markScheme: 1 mark: the material is the independent variable
1 mark: keeping the shape the same makes it a fair test / so differences are due to the material only
questions.explanation: To compare how different substances refract light, everything except the material must be kept the same, including the angle of incidence and block shape.

questions.question: When light passes through a glass window, explain why you can also see a faint reflection of yourself in it, especially at night.
acceptedAnswers: less light from outside at night
markScheme: 1 mark: at the boundary some light is reflected while most is transmitted
1 mark: at night little light comes through from outside, so the reflected light is easier to see
questions.explanation: Boundaries usually reflect part of a wave and transmit the rest. The faint reflection is normally swamped by light from outside during the day.

questions.question: Describe how to draw a ray diagram to show the reflection of a ray of light from a plane mirror. Include how the angles are measured.
markScheme: Indicative content:
draw the mirror as a straight line (hatched on the back)
mark the point where the incident ray meets the mirror
draw the normal at 90° to the mirror at that point, as a dashed line, using a protractor
draw the incident ray with an arrow towards the mirror
measure angle of incidence between incident ray and normal
draw reflected ray at the same angle on the other side of the normal, with arrow away from the mirror
angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence including the normal and equal angles measured from the normal.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct features, for example i = r, but the normal or measurement method is missing.
questions.explanation: The essential features are the normal at 90°, angles measured from the normal, i = r, and arrows on rays.

questions.question: Required practical 9. Describe a method to investigate how light is refracted by blocks of different transparent materials. Include the equipment, the measurements and how to make the results valid.
markScheme: Indicative content:
equipment: ray box with single slit, power supply, rectangular blocks (glass, acrylic / Perspex), protractor, ruler, sharp pencil, white paper
work in a darkened room
place block on paper and draw around it
draw a normal at 90° to one face
shine a ray at a measured angle of incidence (e.g. 40°) to the normal where it meets the block
mark the incident and emerging rays with crosses; remove block and join the points to show the ray inside the block
measure the angle of refraction between the ray in the block and the normal
repeat for other angles of incidence and for each material
control variables: same angle of incidence, same shape / size of block, same ray box
repeat measurements and calculate means; compare angles of refraction for each material
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, detailed method that would give valid results, including measurement of both angles from the normal and control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): method with key steps but limited detail on measurement or control.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements; method not workable.
questions.explanation: A valid method changes only the material, keeps the angle of incidence the same, and measures all angles from the normal.

questions.question: Which word describes a wave passing through a material and continuing on the other side?
options: Absorbed
Reflected
Transmitted
Emitted
markScheme: 1 mark: Transmitted
questions.explanation: Transmission means the wave passes through. Absorbed waves transfer their energy to the material; reflected waves bounce back.

questions.question: Rays of light from a ray box hit a plane mirror at angles of incidence of 20°, 40° and 60°. Which graph would the student expect when plotting angle of reflection against angle of incidence?
options: A straight line through the origin with a gradient of 2
A straight line through the origin with a gradient of 1
A curve that levels off at 90°
A horizontal straight line
markScheme: 1 mark: A straight line through the origin with a gradient of 1
questions.explanation: Since r = i for every angle, the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.

questions.question: In a ray diagram, state what the arrow on a ray shows.
markScheme: 1 mark: the direction in which the light (wave) is travelling
questions.explanation: Arrows show the direction of travel, so you can tell the incident ray from the reflected ray.

questions.question: A student shines a ray of light along the normal onto a glass block. Describe what happens to the ray at the boundary.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is transmitted without changing direction (no refraction)
1 mark: a small amount is reflected straight back along the normal
questions.explanation: A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°, so it does not bend; a little light is still reflected back along the same line.

questions.question: Required practical 9. Suggest three ways a student could reduce errors when measuring angles of refraction through a glass block.
markScheme: 1 mark: use a narrow ray / darkened room so the ray is clear
1 mark: mark the ray with crosses far apart and use a sharp pencil
1 mark: repeat the measurement and calculate a mean / check the normal is at 90° with a protractor
questions.explanation: Any three sensible improvements that make the ray easier to locate or the angles more accurate gain credit.

questions.question: Light hits a matt black surface. What happens to most of the light?
options: It is absorbed
It is reflected in one direction
It is transmitted
It is scattered and reflected
markScheme: 1 mark: It is absorbed
questions.explanation: Matt black surfaces absorb most of the light falling on them, which is why they look black and warm up in sunlight.
